Coming from CoordinateCleaner

Source: vignettes/coordinatecleaner.Rmd
coordinatecleaner.Rmd

OccurrenceCleaner runs the record tests of CoordinateCleaner (Zizka et al. 2019) with the same definitions and default buffers, and writes the result as flags instead of filtering. This article maps each CoordinateCleaner function to its test here, runs both packages on the same records, lists every case where the flags differ and why, and names the CoordinateCleaner functions that have no counterpart. The chunks that call CoordinateCleaner run only when it is installed; it is a suggested package, not a dependency.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/OccurrenceCleaner")

Needs a C++ compiler (Rtools on Windows).

library(OccurrenceCleaner)

Function mapping

CoordinateCleaner OccurrenceCleaner
cc_val() invalid
cc_zero() zero
cc_equ() equal
cc_cap() capital
cc_cen() centroid
cc_inst() institution
cc_gbif() gbif_headquarters
cc_sea() sea
cc_urb() urban
cc_coun() country_mismatch
cc_dupl() duplicate
cf_equal() age_equal
clean_coordinates() flag_occurrences(x, tests = …)
buffer arguments (capitals_rad, …) buffers = list(capital = …)
ref arguments (cc_cap(ref = …), cc_sea(ref = …), …) gazetteers = list(capital = …, sea = …)
cf_range(method = “time”, max_range = …) tally_flags(bins = …) on max_ma - min_ma
additions (cc_dupl) duplicate_by
seas_scale (default 50) land_scale (default 110, as cc_sea())
value = “clean” x[!has_flag(x$flags, rule), ]
value = “flagged” / “spatialvalid” the flag_ columns

Every test is chosen by name through the tests argument of the one verb, flag_occurrences(), so there are no cc_* functions in this package; with both attached, CoordinateCleaner’s functions keep their names.

Both clean_coordinates() and flag_occurrences() choose their tests by name through a tests argument. CoordinateCleaner’s names are plural (“capitals”), the names here singular (“capital”):

CoordinateCleaner OccurrenceCleaner
capitals capital
centroids centroid
countries country_mismatch
duplicates duplicate
equal equal
gbif gbif_headquarters
institutions institution
seas sea
urban urban
zeros zero

The check for missing or out-of-range coordinates has no name in clean_coordinates(). It always runs first, and if any coordinate fails it, clean_coordinates() stops and returns that result alone. Here it is the invalid test, and the other tests still run on the records that pass it.

Side by side

A typical CoordinateCleaner pipeline filters as it goes, each cc_*() call dropping the records it flags:

library(CoordinateCleaner)
clean <- x |>
  cc_val() |>
  cc_equ() |>
  cc_zero() |>
  cc_cap() |>
  cc_cen() |>
  cc_inst() |>
  cc_gbif() |>
  cc_sea()

The same cleaning here is one flagging call and one subset. The subset can be changed later without flagging again:

f <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "equal", "zero", "capital", "centroid",
                                   "institution", "gbif_headquarters", "sea"))
clean <- f[!has_flag(f$flags, c("invalid", "equal", "zero", "capital", "centroid",
                                "institution", "gbif_headquarters", "sea")), ]

clean_coordinates() is the closer equivalent, since it also returns one column per test rather than dropping records. Its columns are TRUE for records that pass, the flag_<test> columns here are TRUE for records that fail. Records within 30 km of five capitals, plus 20 zeros, 20 equal coordinates and 10 records within 0.3 degrees of (0, 0), run through both:

set.seed(3)
caps <- cbind(lon = c(16.37, 2.35, -3.70, 13.40, 69.17), lat = c(48.21, 48.86, 40.42, 52.52, 34.53))
k <- sample(5, 4000, TRUE)
p <- geosphere::destPoint(caps[k, ], b = runif(4000, 0, 360), d = 30000 * sqrt(runif(4000)))
x <- data.frame(species = sample(c("a", "b"), 4000, TRUE),
                decimalLongitude = round(p[, 1], 4), decimalLatitude = round(p[, 2], 4))
x[1:20, 2:3] <- 0
x[21:40, 3] <- x[21:40, 2]
x[41:50, 2:3] <- round(runif(20, -0.3, 0.3), 4)
cc <- CoordinateCleaner::clean_coordinates(
  x, lon = "decimalLongitude", lat = "decimalLatitude", species = "species",
  tests = c("capitals", "centroids", "equal", "gbif", "institutions", "zeros", "duplicates"),
  value = "spatialvalid", verbose = FALSE)
oc <- flag_occurrences(x, tests = c("invalid", "zero", "equal", "capital", "centroid",
                                    "institution", "gbif_headquarters", "duplicate"),
                       reference = "CoordinateCleaner")

reference = "CoordinateCleaner" reads that package’s own gazetteers at run time, so both packages test against the same points. Per test, the share of records with the same verdict:

pairs <- c(.zer = "zero", .equ = "equal", .cap = "capital", .cen = "centroid",
           .inst = "institution", .gbf = "gbif_headquarters", .dpl = "duplicate")
agree <- vapply(names(pairs), function(cn)
  mean((!cc[[cn]]) == oc[[paste0("flag_", pairs[[cn]])]], na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1))
knitr::kable(data.frame(CoordinateCleaner = names(pairs), OccurrenceCleaner = pairs,
                        flagged_cc = vapply(names(pairs), function(cn) sum(!cc[[cn]], na.rm = TRUE), 1),
                        flagged_oc = vapply(pairs, function(t) sum(oc[[paste0("flag_", t)]]), 1),
                        agreement = round(agree, 5)), row.names = FALSE)
CoordinateCleaner OccurrenceCleaner flagged_cc flagged_oc agreement
.zer zero 20 30 0.99750
.equ equal 40 40 1.00000
.cap capital 435 436 0.99975
.cen centroid 29 29 1.00000
.inst institution 0 0 1.00000
.gbf gbif_headquarters 0 0 1.00000
.dpl duplicate 18 18 1.00000

The two differ in zero, on purpose, for the 10 records near but not at (0, 0), and in capital for records at the buffer edge; the next section explains both. The package’s own test suite runs this comparison on sampled records for every equivalent test and requires the differences to be only those documented below.

Where the flags differ

Buffer circles

CoordinateCleaner builds each buffer as a polygon with its vertices on the circle (72 vertices for capitals, centroids and the GBIF headquarters, 40 for institutions) and tests whether a record lies inside that polygon. Between two vertices the polygon edge lies inside the circle, at rcos⁡(π/n)r \cos(\pi / n) from the centre at mid-edge: 99.9 % of the buffer for 72 vertices, 99.7 % for 40. OccurrenceCleaner tests the geodesic distance against the buffer itself. A record due north of Kabul’s capital point (a vertex direction) and one at a bearing of 2.5 degrees (mid-edge), each at 9,995 m:

e <- new.env(); utils::data("countryref", package = "CoordinateCleaner", envir = e)
kabul <- unlist(e$countryref[e$countryref$iso3 == "AFG", c("capital.lon", "capital.lat")][1, ])
p <- geosphere::destPoint(kabul, b = c(0, 2.5), d = 9995)
y <- data.frame(species = "a", decimalLongitude = p[, 1], decimalLatitude = p[, 2])
data.frame(bearing = c(0, 2.5), distance_m = 9995,
           cc_flagged = !CoordinateCleaner::cc_cap(y, value = "flagged", verbose = FALSE),
           oc_flagged = flag_occurrences(y, tests = "capital", reference = "CoordinateCleaner")$flag_capital)
#>   bearing distance_m cc_flagged oc_flagged
#> 1     0.0       9995       TRUE       TRUE
#> 2     2.5       9995      FALSE       TRUE

So every record CoordinateCleaner flags is flagged here, and the extra flags are records between 99.7 % and 100 % of a buffer: within 9.5 m of the 10 km capital edge, 0.95 m of the 1 km centroid and headquarters edge, 0.31 m of the 100 m institution edge.

The zero buffer

CoordinateCleaner’s cc_zero() documents a 0.5-degree buffer around (0, 0). In version 3.0.1 the buffer point is created without a coordinate reference system, terra assumes longitude and latitude, and terra::buffer(width = 0.5) then buffers 0.5 metres. Only records with a longitude or latitude of exactly zero are flagged:

z <- data.frame(species = "a", decimalLongitude = c(0, 0.3, 0.001), decimalLatitude = c(12, 0.3, 0.001))
data.frame(z[, 2:3],
           cc_flagged = !CoordinateCleaner::cc_zero(z, value = "flagged", verbose = FALSE),
           oc_flagged = flag_occurrences(z, tests = "zero")$flag_zero,
           oc_zero_buffer_0 = flag_occurrences(z, tests = "zero", buffers = list(zero = 0))$flag_zero)
#>   decimalLongitude decimalLatitude cc_flagged oc_flagged oc_zero_buffer_0
#> 1            0.000          12.000       TRUE       TRUE             TRUE
#> 2            0.300           0.300      FALSE       TRUE            FALSE
#> 3            0.001           0.001      FALSE       TRUE            FALSE

This package applies the documented 0.5-degree radius. buffers = list(zero = 0) reproduces CoordinateCleaner 3.0.1’s results.

Country codes

cc_coun() compares the record’s code with the ISO alpha-3 code of the country polygon only. GBIF’s countryCode is alpha-2, so a GBIF table needs converting first. country_mismatch accepts alpha-2, alpha-3 and Natural Earth’s ADM0_A3 code, which fills the gaps where Natural Earth has -99 for the ISO code. For records whose code is alpha-3 and present in Natural Earth, the two tests agree.

Records without valid coordinates

For rows with missing or out-of-range coordinates, CoordinateCleaner’s spatial tests return NA (cc_zero, cc_equ) or “clean” (cc_cap), and cc_dupl flags the second of two such rows. Here such a record gets the invalid bit and no other spatial bit, so a rule that holds invalid removes it and a rule without invalid sees no spatial flag on it.

Duplicates in streamed input

On a data frame duplicate is evaluated over the whole table, as cc_dupl() is. On a table streamed from disk it is evaluated within each input file; the on-disk article shows how to make the files the right units for that.

Gazetteers

With the default reference = "natural_earth" the gazetteers are rebuilt from the original sources (Natural Earth, GBIF’s registry of collections), not copied from CoordinateCleaner, whose code and data are GPL-3. They hold the same kinds of points but not the same coordinates; the reference-data article measures the differences. reference = "CoordinateCleaner" uses CoordinateCleaner’s tables and reproduces its flags up to the differences above.

Speed

The proximity tests are where the two packages differ most, because CoordinateCleaner builds a polygon per reference point and tests each record against all of them, while this package queries a kd-tree. Measured on one machine (AMD Ryzen 7 5700G, 64 GB, Windows, R 4.6.1, OccurrenceCleaner 0.1.0, CoordinateCleaner 3.0.1), single process, both reading CoordinateCleaner’s gazetteers, in seconds:

test OccurrenceCleaner, 1e6 CoordinateCleaner, 1e6 OccurrenceCleaner, 1e7 CoordinateCleaner, 1e7
capital 0.28 24.5 1.78 242.3
centroid 0.15 34.9 2.15 246.2
institution 0.18 1.0 1.73 7.4
gbif_headquarters 0.08 0.6 0.81 6.5
sea 0.06 5.9 0.66 59.7
zero 0.07 0.6 0.42 6.7
equal 0.03 0.0 0.36 0.1
invalid 0.02 5.9 0.38 64.3
duplicate 1.55 1.1 13.79 11.9
default_tests() (own reference) 1.90 not run 17.79 not run

At ten million records the capital test takes 1.8 s here and 242 s in CoordinateCleaner, the centroid test 2.2 s and 246 s. The equal and duplicate tests are plain vector operations in both packages and take about the same time. Beyond memory, an on-disk table is streamed in chunks (see the on-disk article), so the input size is bounded by disk space only. The benchmark script is bench/benchmark.R in the source repository.

What has no counterpart

CoordinateCleaner also has the functions below, which have no counterpart in OccurrenceCleaner 0.1.0. For them CoordinateCleaner remains the tool, and its result can be combined with the flags here by joining on a record identifier.

CoordinateCleaner function what it does
cc_outl() spatial outliers per species (distance or quantile methods)
cc_iucn() records outside a species’ range polygon
cc_aohi() records in an artificial hotspot occurrence inventory
cd_ddmm(), cd_round() dataset-level tests for degree-minute conversion errors and rasterised sampling
clean_dataset() runs the dataset-level tests
cf_age(), cf_outl(), cf_range(method = “quantile” or “mad”) fossil age and range outliers per taxon
write_pyrate() export to PyRate

cc_outl() compares each record with the other records of the same species, so its result depends on the whole species sample and changes when records are added or removed; the tests here are record tests whose flag depends only on the record itself and pinned reference data. The same holds for the per-taxon fossil tests. cf_equal() is a record test and is ported as age_equal; the fossil article shows it and the age-range bins on a fossil table.

References

Zizka A, Silvestro D, Andermann T, Azevedo J, Duarte Ritter C, Edler D, Farooq H, Herdean A, Ariza M, Scharn R, Svanteson S, Wengström N, Zizka V, Antonelli A (2019). CoordinateCleaner: standardized cleaning of occurrence records from biological collection databases. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 10:744-751. doi:10.1111/2041-210X.13152
